issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising second-appeal jurisdiction cannot reappreciate properly supported findings of fact in the absence of a substantial question of law or perversity, illegality, or irregularity.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court found that possession had been delivered for cultivation on a permissive basis, not under a sale.
Both courts found no proof of a sale agreement or of hostile possession.
Those findings were based on their assessment of the evidence and were not shown to be perverse, illegal, or irregular.
The High Court reappreciated the evidence and displaced those findings in a second appeal.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded the limits of second-appeal jurisdiction by interfering with the concurrent findings of fact; its judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure confines a High Court’s second-appeal jurisdiction to cases involving a substantial question of law and does not authorize interference with pure questions of fact. The Court relied on the concurrent factual findings and held that they disclosed no perversity, illegality, or irregularity warranting interference.

rule.if: second_appeal_proceeding and concurrent_findings_based_on_evidence and not findings_perverse_or_illegal_or_irregular

predicates.second_appeal_proceeding: The matter is an appeal to a High Court from a first appellate court’s decision.
predicates.concurrent_findings_based_on_evidence: The trial court and first appellate court reached the same factual findings after assessing the evidence.
predicates.findings_perverse_or_illegal_or_irregula: The concurrent factual findings are shown to be perverse, illegal, or irregular.

issues.definition: When a matter is a second appeal and both lower courts have made evidence-based factual findings that are not shown to be perverse, illegal, or irregular, the High Court must not reweigh those facts.

issues.legal_issue: Permissive possession does not become adverse possession through duration alone; the possessor must establish hostile possession and hostile animus to the knowledge of the owner.
material_facts: The land was delivered to the defendant for cultivation on a share-cropping basis for a limited period.
The defendant remained in possession, but the lower courts found no evidence that he asserted a hostile title against the owner.
Revenue records supported the finding that the possession was permissive and that the plaintiff remained the owner.
The defendant relied on the alleged sale as the basis of entry, but the alleged sale was not proved.
issues.conclusion: The defendant did not acquire title by adverse possession because he failed to establish when or how his permissive possession became hostile to the owner.
issues.legal_principle: A person whose possession began permissively must prove, by cogent and convincing evidence, hostile animus and possession adverse to the knowledge of the real owner; mere long possession does not convert permissive possession into adverse possession. The Court relied on Thakur Kishan Singh (Dead) v. Arvind Kumar, (1994) 6 SCC 591.

rule.if: adverse_possession_claim and permissive_entry and not hostile_animus_proved

predicates.adverse_possession_claim: A person claims title to property by adverse possession.
predicates.permissive_entry: The person entered or remained in possession with the owner's permission or under an arrangement that did not assert ownership against the owner.
predicates.hostile_animus_proved: The person proves an assertion of hostile title and possession adverse to the owner's knowledge.

issues.definition: A claim based on adverse possession fails where possession began permissively and hostile animus is not proved.

issues.legal_issue: A claim to retain possession under part performance of an agreement and a claim of adverse possession are inconsistent where the possessor relies on lawful entry under the agreement without proving a later hostile assertion of ownership.
material_facts: The defendant relied on an alleged agreement to sale as the basis for lawful possession and also claimed title by adverse possession.
The alleged sale agreement was not proved, and the lower courts found that possession had instead been delivered for cultivation.
There was no evidence that the defendant later asserted hostile ownership against the plaintiff.
issues.conclusion: The adverse-possession plea was unavailable on the basis of the asserted lawful entry under the agreement unless a later hostile assertion of possession as owner was established.
issues.legal_principle: A plea of adverse possession is inconsistent with retaining possession under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act where the possessor accepts lawful entry under an agreement and continued possession under it; adverse possession may be available only if hostile animus after entry is asserted and proved. The Court relied on Mohan Lal v. Mirza Abdul Gaffar, (1996) 1 SCC 639.

rule.if: part_performance_defense and adverse_possession_claim and lawful_entry_under_agreement and not later_hostile_assertion_proved

predicates.part_performance_defense: A person relies on part performance of an agreement as a basis for retaining possession of property.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim: The person also claims title to the property by adverse possession.
predicates.lawful_entry_under_agreement: The person asserts that possession began lawfully under the agreement.
predicates.later_hostile_assertion_proved: The person proves a later assertion of hostile ownership after entering possession.

issues.definition: Where a person relies on lawful entry under an agreement and also claims adverse possession, the latter plea is unavailable unless a later hostile assertion is proved.

issues.legal_issue: The contents of an alleged written sale instrument cannot be treated as proved merely from a party’s oral account when the instrument is not produced and its contents are not otherwise established.
material_facts: The defendant alleged that a written sale instrument supported his claim to the land.
The instrument was not produced, and the first appellate court found that no secondary evidence had been sought.
The persons said to have witnessed the transaction were not called to prove it.
The High Court relied on the defendant’s oral account of the alleged sale despite those evidentiary deficiencies.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not treat the alleged contents of the unproduced instrument as established by relying on the defendant’s oral account.
issues.legal_principle: Where an alleged written instrument is not on the record, its alleged contents cannot be established merely by referring to a party’s oral account; the Court identified no particular statutory provision for this holding.

predicates.written_sale_claim: A person bases a claim to property on an alleged written sale instrument.
predicates.instrument_not_produced: The alleged written instrument is not produced in the proceeding.
predicates.contents_supported_only_by_oral_account: The alleged contents of the instrument are supported only by a party’s oral account.

issues.definition: When a property claim relies on an unproduced written sale instrument and its alleged contents are supported only by oral account, those contents are not established.
